passed_precedents.title: Konakala Ramakrishna @ Ramu And Others vs State Of A.P. Rep. By Its Public ... on 22 September, 2017
passed_precedents.quote: The other crucial weakness in the case of the prosecution is that all the so-called eye witnesses asserted that Vijaya (A6) and the others threw chilly powder upon D1 and D2. However, P.W.13, the doctor who conducted the post-mortem examination of the bodies of D1 and D2, categorically stated that he did not notice any chilly powder on any part of the bodies of the two dead persons.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: However, P.W.13, the doctor who conducted the post-mortem examination of the bodies of D1 and D2, categorically stated that he did not notice any chilly powder on any part of the bodies of the two dead persons. This was despite the fact that P.W.13 had read the inquest reports. This single fact is enough to completely discredit the eye-witness testimony of P.Ws.1 to 5 and 8 to this effect.

passed_precedents.text: The offense may be treated as culpable homicide under the exception for sudden provocation and heat of passion, lacking premeditation, thus attracting a lesser penalty.
passed_precedents.title: Raval Shaileshbhai Rameshbhai ... vs State Of Gujarat on 17 February, 2026
passed_precedents.quote: The record shows that the quarrel erupted suddenly from what began as mutual joking and exchange of abuses, with no prior enmity or premeditation on record. The accused is said to have become provoked only after the deceased refused to retaliate with similar abuses, leading to the impulsive act of pulling out the knife from his pocket and inflicting multiple blows in the heat of passion.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: In these circumstances, while the act undoubtedly amounts to culpable homicide, the absence of clear evidence of pre-planned intention to cause death, coupled with the sudden quarrel and heat of passion, brings the case within the scope of Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC, thereby attracting punishment under Section 304 Part I IPC rather than Section 302 IPC.

passed_precedents.text: Death resulting from subsequent infection breaks the chain of causation, so the accused cannot be held liable for the death based solely on the initial stabbing.
passed_precedents.title: Chilla Rambabu vs The State Of Andhra Pradesh Rep. By Its ... on 15 September, 2016
passed_precedents.quote: It is however not in dispute that Appala Reddy died nearly three months later, on 03.02.2009, at King George Hospital, Visakhapatnam. The cause of his death was septic and toxic shock due to multiple infected wounds. In effect, his death cannot be directly attributed to the stab injuries sustained by him on 08.11.2008 as it was the intervening infection that led to the septic and toxic shock, which were responsible for his death.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: In effect, his death cannot be directly attributed to the stab injuries sustained by him on 08.11.2008 as it was the intervening infection that led to the septic and toxic shock, which were responsible for his death. No medical evidence is adduced to the effect that despite proper treatment, Appala Reddy would not have survived the said stab injuries. In consequence, this Court holds that the death of Papayamma was indubitably homicidal in nature but the death of Appala Reddy was not so.

passed_precedents.text: The prosecution must prove harassment with specific details; vague and general allegations lacking manner or instances are insufficient.
passed_precedents.title: St. vs . Rahul Verma Etc. on 12 July, 2018
passed_precedents.quote: It is interesting to note that neither in his statement Ex. PW4/A made to the SDM on 29.12.2011 nor in his deposition recorded before the court, PW4 disclosed anything about any demand of Rs.3 lacs or a house at Noida by the accused persons nor there is any specific allegation relating to cruelty or harassment. Though in the statement Ex. PW4/A it was alleged that the husband used to physically assault her whenever deceased complained about the conduct of her in laws in taunting her for not bringing sufficient dowry but, his deposition in the court is totally silent about any such allegation. The allegation of harassment are bald and general as neither the manner of harassment has been disclosed nor any specific instance has been mentioned by PW4 in his deposition.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: The general allegation of harassment without describing the exact conduct of accused will not be sufficient to attract the provisions of Section 498A or 304-B IPC . In this regard, I also refer the judgment in Amar Singh vs. State of Rajasthan 2010 (4) Criminal Court Cases 234 (SC) wherein it was held that " a prosecution witness who merely uses the word "harassed" or "tortured" and does not describe the exact conduct of accused which, according to him, amounted to harassment or torture may not be believed by the court in cases u/s 498A and 304-B IPC."

passed_precedents.text: Delay in adding a serious charge and prosecutorial inaction weakens the case and supports granting anticipatory bail.
passed_precedents.title: Bhadresh Bipinbhai Sheth vs State Of Gujarat & Anr on 1 September, 2015
passed_precedents.quote: Merely because the charge under Section 376 IPC, which is a serious charge, is now added, the benefit of anticipatory bail cannot be denied when such a charge is added after a long period of time and inaction of the prosecutrix is also a contributory factor.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: In a matter like this where allegations of rape pertain to the period which is almost 17 years ago and when no charge was framed under Section 376 IPC in the year 2001, and even the prosecutrix did not take any steps for almost 9 years and the charge under Section 376 IPC is added only in the year 2014, we see no reason why the appellant should not be given the benefit of anticipatory bail. Merely because the charge under Section 376 IPC, which is a serious charge, is now added, the benefit of anticipatory bail cannot be denied when such a charge is added after a long period of time and inaction of the prosecutrix is also a contributory factor.

From his mere failure to subsequently keep a promise, one cannot presume that he all along had a culpable intention to break the prom
passed_precedents.judge_quote: Therefore, it is the intention which is the gist of the offence. To hold a person guilty of cheating it is necessary to show that he had a fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise. From his mere failure to subsequently keep a promise, one cannot presume that he all along had a culpable intention to break the promise from the beginning.

passed_precedents.text: Anticipatory bail may be granted based on the nature and gravity of the accusation, the applicant's antecedents, flight risk, and whether the accusation aims to injure or humiliate the applicant.
passed_precedents.title: Lavesh vs State (Nct Of Delhi) on 31 August, 2012
passed_precedents.quote: Where any person has reason to believe that he may be arrested on accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence, he may apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under this section that in the event of such arrest he shall be released on bail; and that Court may, after taking into consideration, inter alia, the following factors, namely:- i) the nature and gravity of the accusation; ii) the antecedents of the applicant including the fact as to whether he has previously undergone imprisonment on conviction by a Court in respect of any cognizable offence; iii) the possibility of the applicant to flee from justice; and iv) where the accusation has been made with the object of injuring or humiliating the applicant by having him so arrested, either reject the application forthwith or issue an interim order for the grant of anticipatory bail
passed_precedents.judge_quote: The belief that the applicant may be arrested must be founded on reasonable grounds. While considering such a request, the Court has to take into consideration the nature and the gravity of the accusation, antecedents, possibility of the applicant to flee from justice etc.

passed_precedents.text: If the accused resides outside the magistrate's territorial jurisdiction, the magistrate must postpone proceedings and investigate before issuing process.
passed_precedents.title: M/S. Nishka Properties (Pvt.) Ltd. & Anr vs The State Of West Bengal & Anr on 7 August, 2013
passed_precedents.quote: Section 202 of the Code of Criminal Procedure states that any Magistrate, on receipt of a complaint which has been made over to him under Section 192 , shall, in a case where the accused is residing at a place beyond the area in which he exercises his jurisdiction, postpone the issue of process against the accused and either inquire into the case himself or direct an investigation to be made by a police officer or by such other person as he thinks fit, for the purpose of deciding whether or not there is sufficient ground for proceeding.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: Section 202 of the Code of Criminal Procedure states that any Magistrate, on receipt of a complaint which has been made over to him under Section 192 , shall, in a case where the accused is residing at a place beyond the area in which he exercises his jurisdiction, postpone the issue of process against the accused and either inquire into the case himself or direct an investigation to be made by a police officer or by such other person as he thinks fit, for the purpose of deciding whether or not there is sufficient ground for proceeding. It is thus apparent that in cases where the accused resides outside the territorial jurisdiction of the Court of the Magistrate, the learned Magistrate is required either to inquire himself or to direct investigation by a police officer or any other person deemed fit by the learned Magistrate.

passed_precedents.text: The charge for dowry harassment under section 498A cannot be sustained when the complaint lacks specific particulars of time and nature of demand.
passed_precedents.title: Anwar Beig vs State on 3 June, 2022
passed_precedents.quote: Mr. Pankaj Jain, learned counsel appearing for revisionists submitted that that learned Trial Court has committed grave illegality by framing charge under section 406 and 498A read with section 34 of the IPC against the revisionists as statement of the complainant is very general regarding dowry. Insofar as, the demand of dowry and the harassment are concerned, no particulars were given as to the time and nature of demand.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: In my view, these allegations are not sufficient to frame charge against the revisionist no. 1 for the offence under section 498A of the IPC. There are no specific allegations against him that he used to demand dowry or used to beat or harass the complainant. He himself did not demand the dowry. He only stated that his son was right and she should ask her mother to give motorcycle. The complainant has not specified the abuses. The general allegations are levelled against the revisionist no. 1. Furthermore, no specific and distinct allegations have been made against the revisionist no. 1. The revisionist no. 1 has not been attributed any specific role in furtherance of the general allegations made against them. The allegations against the revisionist no. 1 are therefore general and omnibus and can at best be said to have been made out on account of small skirmishes.

passed_precedents.quote: One should not overlook the fact that there is Section-18 in the Atrocities Act, which imposes a bar so far as the grant of anticipatory bail is concerned, if the offence is one under the Atrocities Act.

passed_precedents.text: The bar on anticipatory bail under the Atrocities Act creates unequal treatment compared to other serious offences.
passed_precedents.title: Dr. Subhash Kashinath Mahajan vs The State Of Maharashtra on 20 March, 2018
passed_precedents.quote: If a person is accused having committed murder, dacoity, rape, etc., he can pray for anticipatory bail under Section-438 of the Cr.P.C. on the ground that he is innocent and has been falsely involved, but if a person alleged to have committed an offence under the Atrocities Act, cannot pray for an anticipatory bail because of the bar of Section-18 of the Act, and he would get arrested.

passed_precedents.text: The court may grant bail to an accused of a non‑bailable offence if it finds that the prosecution has not made out a prima facie case or if it is satisfied, for reasons to be recorded, that release is required despite a prima facie case.
passed_precedents.title: Satish Singh vs State Of Himachal Pradesh on 29 June, 2020
passed_precedents.quote: But even persons accused of non-bailable offences are entitled for bail if the court concerned comes to the conclusion that the prosecution has failed to establish a prima facie case against him and/or if the court is satisfied for reasons to be recorded that in spite of the existence of prima facie case there is a need to release such persons on bail where fact situations require it to do so.

passed_precedents.quote: These conditions therefore cannot be permitted to stand and are set aside.

passed_precedents.text: A criminal court cannot impose bail conditions aimed at recovering alleged dues; such conditions exceed its jurisdiction.
passed_precedents.title: Mahersing Or His Sucessor In Office ... vs Pradipkumar Bharatlal Poddar Director ... on 24 September, 2003
passed_precedents.quote: It has to be remembered that these are criminal proceedings, and while considering the question of bail, the Court may not exercise the power in a manner to recover the amount.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: Discretionary power of Court to impose conditions while releasing an accused on bail are to be exercised with judicial discretion. A criminal court cannot exercise such powers for recovery of amount.

passed_precedents.text: Under Sections 441 and 445 CrPC, the court cannot mandate cash security; the accused may optionally deposit money in lieu of bond, subject to the court’s discretion.
passed_precedents.title: Mahersing Or His Sucessor In Office ... vs Pradipkumar Bharatlal Poddar Director ... on 24 September, 2003
passed_precedents.quote: The option is with the person who is required to execute bond with or without surety to seek permission of the Court for cash security in lieu of execution of bond and thereupon the discretion is with the Court either to grant or refuse such permission. Differently put, the provisions do not empower the Court to impose a condition for cash surety.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: It is thus very clear that section 441 Cr. P.C. does not contemplate cash deposit. Section 445 Cr. P.C. firstly gives the option to the accused to offer cash security in lieu of executing a bond and then the discretion is with the Court either to permit such cash deposit or to refuse it but the Court on its own cannot direct deposit of cash security.

passed_precedents.text: A person may be charged only when the allegations against him are established prima facie; courts must be cautious before framing charges to avoid affecting liberty and causing unnecessary harassment.
passed_precedents.title: S. Bangarappa vs Ganesh Narayan Hegade And Others on 16 June, 1992
passed_precedents.quote: The Courts below should have borne in mind that a person can be charged only when the allegations alleged against him are established prima facie and not otherwise, because in criminal cases the Courts must be very cautious and careful before proceeding to frame charge as unnecessary framing of charge, on the one hand may result in affecting the person's liberty and on the other hand cause continuous and unnecessary harassment, as it has happened in the instant case.

passed_precedents.text: A conviction for cheating requires proof of fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of the act; mere subsequent failure does not establish that intention.
passed_precedents.title: Inder Mohan Goswami & Another vs State Of Uttaranchal & Others on 9 October, 2007
passed_precedents.quote: To hold a person guilty of cheating it is necessary to show that he had a fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise. From his mere failure to subsequently keep a promise, one cannot presume that he all along had a culpable intention to break the promise from the beginning.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: Therefore, it is the intention which is the gist of the offence. To hold a person guilty of cheating it is necessary to show that he had a fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise. From his mere failure to subsequently keep a promise, one cannot presume that he all along had a culpable intention to break the promise from the beginning.

passed_precedents.text: The offence is complete upon the making of the false document with the requisite intent, regardless of whether the document is actually used for cheating.

passed_precedents.text: To convict someone of using a forged document as genuine, the prosecution must show that the person knew the document was forged, used it as genuine, and acted with fraudulent or dishonest intent.
passed_precedents.title: State vs Dalip Kumar Etc on 30 May, 2026
passed_precedents.quote: The essential ingredients are: (i) using a document known to be forged; (ii) using it as genuine; and (iii) fraudulent or dishonest intent. The knowledge that the document is forged is an essential ingredient, which may be inferred from the circumstances of the case.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: Section 471 IPC/ Using as Genuine a Forged Document: The essential ingredients are: (i) using a document known to be forged; (ii) using it as genuine; and (iii) fraudulent or dishonest intent. The knowledge that the document is forged is an essential ingredient, which may be inferred from the circumstances of the case.

passed_precedents.text: An employee who neither participated in the relevant process nor possessed UPSI cannot be held liable for insider trading.
passed_precedents.title: Piramal Enterprises Limited vs Sebi on 15 May, 2019
passed_precedents.quote: The AO found that the said employee was not associated in any manner with the process of domestic healthcare business and was not in possession of the Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) relating to the deal. The AO accordingly exonerated 28 him of the charge of insider trading.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: SEBI had made an investigation and found that only one designated employee had traded in the scrips. The AO found that the said employee was not associated in any manner with the process of domestic healthcare business and was not in possession of the Unpublished Price Sensitive Information (UPSI) relating to the deal. The AO accordingly exonerated 28 him of the charge of insider trading.

passed_precedents.text: If unpublished price sensitive information is preserved and not misused, there is no insider trading violation.
passed_precedents.title: Piramal Enterprises Limited vs Sebi on 15 May, 2019
passed_precedents.quote: We further find that UPSI at all times was preserved and there was no misuse of UPSI.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: Thus, even though, no announcement was made for closure of the trading window, we find that PEL ensured compliance in pith and substance of the Model Code of PEL and the PIT Regulations including the Model Code. We further find that UPSI at all times was preserved and there was no misuse of UPSI.

passed_precedents.text: A technical breach of the internal model code, without actual misuse of UPSI, does not substantiate an insider trading charge.
passed_precedents.title: Piramal Enterprises Limited vs Sebi on 15 May, 2019
passed_precedents.quote: In the light of the aforesaid, we find that the violation of the Model Code in the given circumstances is technical in nature.
passed_precedents.judge_quote: In the absence of any direct or clinching evidence of insider trading or misuse of UPSI, a reasonable benefit of doubt should be extended to the PEL instead of mechanically imposing a penalty.
